the effects of the various manipulations of the drinking situation on the development of postreinforcement water drinking are not clear-cut and are probably not due to a single factor.

the results of the experiment are consistent with the hypothesis that the development of strong post-reinforcement drinking under variable-interval reinforcement of food depends on the proximity of the lever to the water tube and on the proportion of short interreinforcement intervals.

the development of postreinforcement water drinking is not a simple, unitary phenomenon, but a complex function of many interacting variables, including (a) the amount and distribution of the food reinforcement, (b) the proximity and availability of the drinking tube, (c) the presence or absence of a competing response (i.e., lever pressing) during the interfood period, and (d) the amount of water reinforcement.

the more frequently the animal is reinforced for lever pressing and the closer the water is to the lever, the greater the amount of postreinforcement water consumption.
